title: Pittston Stevedoring Corp. v. Dellaventura
lead: Four waterfront compensation awards reached the Second Circuit after Congress extended federal coverage landward. Two petitions failed at the threshold; the other two required the court to decide how modern cargo handling fit the amended statute.

actors.name: Blundo, Scaffidi, Dellaventura, and Caputo
actors.role: Workers whose compensation awards were challenged

actors.name: International Terminal Operating Company, Pittston, and Northeast Marine Terminal
Benefits Review Board
actors.role: Administrative appellate body that sustained the awards

proceedings: Second Circuit dismissed Dellaventura’s petition as untimely and Scaffidi’s for lack of a justiciable controversy; it denied Blundo’s and Caputo’s petitions on the merits, with Lumbard dissenting only from those merits outcomes.
limits: This account preserves the 1976 statutory and deference framework from the full source brief. Later judgments and current law are outside its scope; no new opinion audit is claimed.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Congress extends waterfront compensation
paragraphs: Congress changed the Longshoremen’s and Harbor Workers’ Compensation Act in 1972. It eliminated longshoremen’s unseaworthiness suits against vessels and prohibited employer-indemnity arrangements underlying the Sieracki–Ryan litigation triangle, the sequence of worker claims and vessel recourse against employers. Negligence suits against vessels remained. Workers received increased benefits and expanded federal coverage.

The old location requirement generally reached navigable waters and dry docks. The amended provision included adjoining piers, wharves, terminals, and other specified vessel-related areas. A new occupational requirement covered maritime employment, including longshoremen, longshoring operations, and specified harbor workers. An eligible location alone therefore did not establish coverage, and Congress left the exact occupational boundary undefined.

sections.title: Four cargo-handling injuries produce awards
paragraphs: Blundo checked cargo for International Terminal Operating Company. A container unloaded at one Brooklyn pier traveled over city streets to another, where Customs opened it and workers stripped its contents. Blundo slipped on ice while checking those contents at the waterfront stringpiece. That finger pier handled containers rather than vessels but adjoined the water.

Scaffidi drove a container-moving hustler for Pittston. After transporting a container over public streets between piers, he was injured when a case fell as the container was opened at the receiving platform before vessel loading. Dellaventura, a sorter who sometimes worked in ship holds, slipped on loose coffee beans while helping load a consignee’s truck. The cargo had been discharged 133 days earlier, with no explanation for the delay. The majority described that pier as lacking warehouse facilities.

Caputo usually did terminal labor and accepted available longshoreman shape-up work. While working for Northeast Marine Terminal, he was injured rolling a dolly of cheese into a consignee’s truck. The cheese had been discharged at least five days earlier. The parties stipulated that the task posed the same risk as comparable truck loading elsewhere. Administrative law judges awarded compensation, and the Benefits Review Board sustained the awards.

sections.title: Two petitions cannot reach statutory coverage
paragraphs: The Board issued Dellaventura’s order on October 9, 1975, but the employer and insurer did not petition until February 5, 1976. Section 921(c) allowed sixty days from issuance. Although the agency apparently failed to notify the parties directly as required by regulation, counsel received the decision within the period and offered no explanation for delay. Issuance controlled. Even assuming an implied excusable-neglect exception, these facts would not justify it. The Second Circuit granted Dellaventura’s dismissal motion without deciding the Solicitor of Labor’s authority to make a parallel motion.

Scaffidi’s insurer paid the award and abandoned the contest. Pittston still sought review, alleging effects on experience ratings and future premiums, but offered only conclusory assertions. More fundamentally, reversal could not recover the voluntary payment, and Pittston identified no effective relief. Unlike a case leaving part of an employer’s liability unpaid, this petition sought an advisory opinion about an already paid award. It too was dismissed.

sections.title: The remaining petitions require statutory interpretation
paragraphs: Employers urged a first/last-point-of-rest rule: unloading coverage ended at cargo’s first resting place after discharge, and loading coverage began at its last resting place before vessel loading. Workers and the government proposed a broader process extending through delivery to, or receipt from, the consignee’s vehicle.

Judge Friendly, joined by Judge Oakes, accepted substantial-evidence review of facts but rejected sustaining statutory coverage merely because the Board’s interpretation was rational. Supreme Court decisions reflected competing approaches to deference. Here, the Board adjudicated rather than made national policy, lacked a comprehensive record of waterfront practices, and had little experience with the amendments. Legislative history and judicial decisions mattered substantially; repetition of early rulings did not create expertise. This differed from substantive rulemaking or interpretation of an agency’s own regulations.

The Act’s factually rebuttable coverage presumption did not answer a general construction question. Definitions used for policing, safety, or cargo liability likewise could not simply be imported. Remedial purpose mattered alongside text, structure, and legislative history. Although Friendly criticized the thin administrative records, the panel decided the pending cases rather than remanding for a comprehensive inquiry, while reserving possible reconsideration if another circuit ordered such an inquiry.

sections.title: Modern cargo operations satisfy both requirements
paragraphs: Text and committee reports treated shore-based container stripping and stuffing as functional parts of vessel unloading and loading. Blundo’s direct participation did not lose its maritime character because the container crossed a street or passed its initial resting place. He met the occupational and location requirements.

Congress also sought uniform coverage for workers whose duties otherwise moved them in and out of the Act. Caputo performed typical vessel-related longshoring, rather than merely collecting stored goods for onward transportation. On these facts, moving cheese into the truck remained part of unloading. The truck’s interior was an artificial boundary, and five days’ delay did not establish excluded storage. Ordinary truck-loading risk did not create a separate task-specific hazard test.

The majority protected at least eligible-location workers stripping or stuffing containers and cargo handlers through departure from the pier who spent a significant part of their work in typical vessel loading or unloading. It reserved whether that occupational proviso was essential and how public warehouses should be treated. It did not cover every worker anywhere in the enlarged area. Congress had constitutional authority to extend maritime compensation onto adjoining structures; maritime employment contracts supplied an additional basis if necessary.

sections.title: The panel enters four distinct outcomes
paragraphs: The court denied the Blundo and Caputo petitions on the merits, leaving those awards intact, while dismissing the Dellaventura and Scaffidi petitions without deciding coverage. Judge Lumbard agreed with the two dismissals but dissented on the merits. He preferred the first/last-point-of-rest rule as faithful to Congress’s correction of water–land anomalies and easier to administer. Because both injuries occurred after the first resting point, he would set aside the awards.

Lumbard described Dellaventura’s cargo as warehouse-stored, unlike the majority’s no-warehouse account. That factual difference did not become a coverage holding because Dellaventura’s petition was untimely.
